claims.text: While a method runs it has a call frame on the stack for its local variables, and the frame goes when the method returns; where the runtime physically puts each slot is left open.
claims.source_hint: GC fundamentals, 'Memory release' (roots include local variables on a thread's stack and CPU registers) and 'Stack roots' (JIT decides the region a stack variable is reported in)

claims.text: Stack memory is taken back with the call frame that owns it — the frame added last is the first one to go — so nothing decides per object when it is released.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals, 'Memory allocation' — the stack is reclaimed with the call frame, unlike the managed heap

claims.text: In .NET 10, an object created with new for a class type is allocated on the managed heap, and the variable it is assigned to holds a reference to it, not the object.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/reference-types: 'a variable of a reference type contains a reference to an object'

claims.text: A heap object stays alive after the method that created it returns, as long as some reference still reaches it.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/standard/garbage-collection/fundamentals, 'Conditions for a garbage collection' and the roots discussion: objects survive while reachable from a root

claims.text: In .NET 10, assigning one variable of a class type to another copies the reference, so both variables reach the same object and a change made through one is seen through the other.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/reference-types — assignment copies the reference; verified by running the stack-heap sample at stage-0

claims.text: In .NET 10, assigning one variable of a value type to another copies the data, so the two are independent and changing one leaves the other as it was.
claims.source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/value-types, 'Value types' — 'a variable of a value type contains an instance of the type'; verified by the same run

claims.text: The garbage collector takes back heap objects the running program can no longer reach, and it chooses when to collect; nothing in this lesson's code makes an object's memory come back at a particular line.
claims.source_hint: GC fundamentals, 'Memory release' (unreachable from roots = garbage; the optimizing engine determines the best time) and 'Conditions for a garbage collection'

claims.text: In .NET 10 you do not free managed heap memory by hand; there is no statement in the lesson's scope that releases one object's memory.

open_questions: The lesson says the sample's local variables belong to the frame for Run and that a value type variable holds the data itself. This is true for the four locals shown, but the general rule 'a value type always lives on the stack' is false (a value type field inside a class object lives inside that object on the heap). depth_notes forbids going further here, so the lesson states only what holds for these locals and never generalises to 'structs are on the stack'. Worth a sentence in a later memory lesson.
